The reproductive biology of the starry weever (Trachinus radiatus) provides insight into its life history strategy, with key parameters estimated from the closely related greater weever, Trachinus draco. At a stable water temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at approximately 8% [GSI = approximately 8%]. This value, derived from comparative studies within the genus, suggests that reproductive investment is balanced against the energetic demands of a benthic predatory lifestyle. The species exhibits a relatively rapid early development; incubation at that same thermal regime produces hatching after an average of 18 days [ab = 18 days], a period during which the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding marks the transition to active larval life at a temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. The duration of this embryonic phase is consistent with the thermal optima observed in other Mediterranean trachinids, where cooler temperatures prolong development but enhance larval survival through more efficient yolk utilization.

Field surveys and growth back-calculations have established that the starry weever reaches a maximum or ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the Trachinidae family inhabiting continental shelf waters. Attaining this asymptotic dimension requires several years of sustained growth, with individuals adding substantial length annually during the warmer months when prey availability is high. The allometric relationship between length and mass, derived from extensive sampling in the Adriatic and Aegean Seas, indicates that an individual of this maximum length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1040 grams [Wwi = approximately 1040 grams]. This pronounced mass gain reflects both skeletal expansion and the accumulation of somatic tissue, particularly in the musculature used for rapid ambush strikes. Such a size trajectory is typical of sit-and-wait predators that must achieve a critical body dimension to effectively subdue relatively large prey items, including small demersal fish and cephalopods. The growth parameters align well with those calculated for the congeneric Trachinus draco, though the starry weever appears to attain a modestly larger terminal size on average.

Sexual maturity in the starry weever is attained at a total length of approximately 21 centimeters [Lp = approximately 21 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds with the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the first capability to participate in annual spawning events. Based on length-at-age data from otolith readings, this length is typically reached around 3.5 years of age, after which individuals begin producing gametes. At this critical size, the predicted wet weight at puberty is about 78.9 grams [Wwp = about 78.9 grams], as calculated from the species-specific length-weight relationship. Reaching this reproductive milestone marks a significant shift in energy allocation, as resources previously directed primarily toward somatic growth are increasingly partitioned into vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males. The modest size at puberty relative to the ultimate length suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction, a common pattern among temperate marine fishes facing moderate adult mortality rates. This strategy allows individuals to contribute to the population well before they approach their maximal physical dimensions, thereby buffering against environmental stochasticity that might otherwise truncate reproductive lifespans.

The earliest life stages of the starry weever are characterized by an exceptionally small initial body mass, a consequence of its pelagic egg production strategy. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from fertilized ova that measure approximately 1.0 millimeter in diameter, yielding a wet weight at birth of just 1.2 milligrams [Wwb = 1.2 milligrams]. This minute starting mass, calculated from the spherical egg volume assuming a standard density for teleost eggs, places the species among those with relatively large buoyant eggs that sustain the embryo through a prolonged endotrophic phase. During the subsequent 18-day incubation period at 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], the developing embryo relies entirely on its yolk reserves, undergoing organogenesis and achieving the mouth-opening stage just as the yolk sac is nearly depleted. The transition to exogenous feeding is a critical bottleneck, as larvae must encounter suitable planktonic prey immediately to avoid the point of no return. This developmental pattern is typical of trachinids, which produce relatively few but well-provisioned eggs compared to other coastal spawners, thereby enhancing larval survival during the vulnerable first-feeding interval in the plankton-rich waters of the Mediterranean.

Lifespan in the starry weever has been estimated from captive observations and field recapture data under controlled thermal conditions at 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], yielding a maximum longevity of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This extended lifespan is relatively long for a medium-sized demersal predator within the Trachinidae family and likely facilitates the iteroparous reproductive strategy observed in the species, with individuals spawning multiple times across successive breeding seasons. The combination of a moderate age at puberty—corresponding to the length of 21 centimeters—and a maximum longevity of 15 years means that a starry weever may reproduce for more than a decade once it reaches sexual maturity. Such a life history schedule buffers population resilience against recruitment failures, as older, larger females produce disproportionately more and higher-quality eggs than their younger counterparts. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 8% [GSI = approximately 8%] at a temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. This pattern aligns with the species' ecological role as a relatively long-lived benthic ambush predator.
